questions.stem: Which of the following grammars is/are ambiguous?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two parse trees for the string a in S to aS or Sa or epsilon, and two parse trees for id plus id times id in E to E plus E or E times E or id

steps.title: What ambiguous means, and the one test
steps.body: A grammar is a set of rewrite rules $A \to \alpha$ that generate strings. A parse tree shows which rule was used at each step. A grammar is ambiguous when at least one string it generates has two different parse trees (equivalently, two different leftmost derivations). The test therefore has one job: either find a string with two trees, or show that at every step the next rule is forced by the string. Here $\epsilon$ is the empty string, and $S \to aS \mid \epsilon$ means $S$ may be replaced by $aS$ or by nothing.

steps.title: Grammars (A) and (D) force every step
steps.body: In (A), $S \to aSb \mid \epsilon$, the string is $a^n b^n$. Look at the string left to write: if it is empty, the only legal rule is $S \to \epsilon$; otherwise it must be $S \to aSb$, because $\epsilon$ would stop too early. The rule at every step is decided, so each string has exactly one tree. In (D), $S \to aS \mid \epsilon$, the string is $a^n$ and the number of letters left again decides: letters left means $aS$, none left means $\epsilon$. Both grammars are unambiguous.

steps.title: Grammar (B): operators with no precedence
steps.body: In (B), $E \to E + E \mid E * E \mid id$, take $id + id * id$. Choosing $+$ as the root operator gives $id + (id * id)$. Choosing $*$ as the root gives $(id + id) * id$. These are two different trees for one string, so (B) is ambiguous. The grammar says nothing about which operator binds tighter, which is exactly the missing precedence and associativity.

steps.title: Grammar (C): the rule can grow from the left or the right
steps.body: In (C), $S \to aS \mid Sa \mid \epsilon$, take the one-letter string $a$. Tree 1: $S \Rightarrow aS \Rightarrow a\epsilon = a$. Tree 2: $S \Rightarrow Sa \Rightarrow \epsilon a = a$. The two trees have different shapes, so (C) is ambiguous. The picture draws both trees for (C) and for the (B) string.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Ambiguous grammars: (B) and (C). This is the official key B;C.

shortcut.body: Scan the rules for two quick red flags. A rule with the same nonterminal at both ends of its right side ($E \to E + E$) or two alternatives that grow from opposite ends ($aS$ and $Sa$) is almost always ambiguous. A rule that is purely right-recursive or has the nonterminal only in the middle with $\epsilon$ at the base ($aSb \mid \epsilon$) is not. Safe for these four; it is only a screen, so always confirm with the two-tree check on the flagged grammars.

traps.text: Calling (A) ambiguous because $S$ sits in the middle and $\epsilon$ is also an alternative. The alternatives are not interchangeable: only the empty remainder can use $\epsilon$, so the tree is unique.
Calling (D) ambiguous because $\epsilon$ is an alternative. Having an empty alternative never creates ambiguity by itself; $a^n$ has one derivation.
Leaving (B) out because the grammar looks like ordinary arithmetic. Without separate levels for $+$ and $*$, the same string groups two ways.
Leaving (C) out because the string looks too simple. The one-letter string $a$ is enough, since $aS$ and $Sa$ both produce it with $S \to \epsilon$.

recognize.clues: The stem asks which of four small grammars are ambiguous, so each needs a two-trees test. Shapes to spot: a rule with the nonterminal at both ends of its right side ($E \to E + E$) and a pair of rules that grow a string from opposite ends ($aS$ and $Sa$).
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse this with left recursion or the LL(1) test. A grammar can be left-recursive and unambiguous, and ambiguity is only settled by two trees for one string, not by the look of a single rule.

check.body: Count parse trees by brute force on short strings. The one-letter string $a$ has 2 trees under $S \to aS \mid Sa \mid \epsilon$ and the string $aa$ has 4, while $aa$ has exactly 1 under $S \to aS \mid \epsilon$ and $aabb$ has exactly 1 under $S \to aSb \mid \epsilon$. The string $id + id * id$ has 2 trees under $E \to E + E \mid E * E \mid id$.

questions.stem: Consider the canonical $LR(0)$ parsing of the grammar below using terminals $\{a, b, c\}$ and non-terminals $\{A, B, C, S\}$ with $S$ as the start symbol. $S \to ACB$; $A \to aA \mid \epsilon$; $C \to cC \mid \epsilon$; $B \to bB \mid b$. Which one of the following options gives the number of shift-reduce conflicts that will occur in the $LR(0)$ ACTION table?

solutionDiagram.alt: Five LR(0) states, each with a complete item beside a shift on the same terminal, giving five shift-reduce conflicts

steps.title: Terms and the rule that makes a conflict
steps.body: An LR(0) item is a production with a dot marking how much of it has been read, for example $A \to a\bullet A$. A state is a set of items the parser can be in at once. In an LR(0) parser the ACTION table is filled without looking ahead: a state holding a complete item (dot at the end, such as $A \to \bullet$ for the empty rule) puts a reduce in every terminal column, and a state with an item that has a terminal after the dot puts a shift in that terminal's column. A shift-reduce conflict is a table cell (state, terminal) that receives both. So the count is the number of (state, terminal) cells that hold a shift and a reduce.

steps.title: Build the states that matter
steps.body: Start: $I_0 = \{S' \to \bullet S,\ S \to \bullet ACB,\ A \to \bullet aA,\ A \to \bullet\}$. After $A$: $I_1 = \{S \to A\bullet CB,\ C \to \bullet cC,\ C \to \bullet\}$. After $a$ from $I_0$ or from itself: $I_3 = \{A \to a\bullet A,\ A \to \bullet aA,\ A \to \bullet\}$. After $c$: $I_5 = \{C \to c\bullet C,\ C \to \bullet cC,\ C \to \bullet\}$. After $b$: $I_8 = \{B \to b\bullet,\ B \to b\bullet B,\ B \to \bullet bB,\ B \to \bullet b\}$.

steps.title: Read the conflicts off each state
steps.body: $I_0$: reduce $A \to \epsilon$ on every terminal, shift $a$. Cell $(I_0, a)$ conflicts. $I_1$: reduce $C \to \epsilon$, shift $c$. Cell $(I_1, c)$ conflicts. $I_3$: reduce $A \to \epsilon$, shift $a$. Cell $(I_3, a)$ conflicts. $I_5$: reduce $C \to \epsilon$, shift $c$. Cell $(I_5, c)$ conflicts. $I_8$: reduce $B \to b$, shift $b$ from $B \to \bullet bB$. Cell $(I_8, b)$ conflicts. The other states hold either only complete items (such as $S \to ACB\bullet$) or only shifts, and none has two reductions, so there are no reduce-reduce conflicts.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Five cells hold a shift and a reduce, so the number of shift-reduce conflicts is $5$, option (D).

shortcut.body: Count by pattern instead of building the automaton. Each nullable nonterminal that is followed by its own recursive terminal start causes a conflict in every state where its rule can begin: $A$ gives $I_0$ and $I_3$ (2), $C$ gives $I_1$ and $I_5$ (2), and the pair $B \to b \mid bB$ gives one more in the state after $b$. Total $2+2+1$. Unsafe when a nonterminal has more than one terminal in its first set, because then each terminal is a separate cell.

traps.text: Answering 2: counting each $\epsilon$-rule ($A$ and $C$) once. $A$ and $C$ each cause a conflict in two states, because the recursive rule $A \to aA$ returns to a state that again starts with $A \to \bullet$.

Answering 3: counting $A$, $C$ and $B$ once each and missing that $I_3$ and $I_5$ repeat the $A$ and $C$ conflicts, so $1+1+1=3$. The state after $a$ ($I_3$) is a separate state from $I_0$ and holds its own conflict.

Answering 4: missing the $B \to b \mid bB$ conflict because $B$ has no $\epsilon$-rule. A conflict needs only a complete item and a shift; $B \to b\bullet$ and $B \to b\bullet B$ sit together in one state.

recognize.clues: The stem says canonical LR(0) and asks for shift-reduce conflicts in the ACTION table. The rules $A \to aA \mid \epsilon$, $C \to cC \mid \epsilon$ and $B \to bB \mid b$ each place a complete item beside a shift on the same letter, which is the shape that makes a cell conflict.
recognize.contrast: SLR(1) uses the same item sets but reduces only on FOLLOW of the left side. Here the question says LR(0), so every complete item reduces on every terminal and FOLLOW sets must not be used to count.

check.body: Switch the reduce rule to SLR and every conflict should vanish. FOLLOW($A$) is $\{b, c\}$, FOLLOW($C$) is $\{b\}$ and FOLLOW($B$) is $\{\$\}$, so reducing $A \to \epsilon$ never lands on the shift letter $a$, reducing $C \to \epsilon$ never lands on $c$, and $B \to b$ never lands on $b$. A run of the SLR(1) test over this grammar reports no conflict at all, so all the conflicts counted come from reducing on every terminal, which is exactly what LR(0) does.

hints.text: A shift-reduce conflict is a cell of the ACTION table, not a state. What must a single cell receive for it to count?

In an LR(0) table a complete item (dot at the end) puts a reduce in every terminal column, whatever the next token is. An item with a terminal right after the dot puts a shift in that terminal's column only.

A conflict therefore needs a complete item and a shift item in the same state. The number of conflicting cells in a state is the number of distinct shift terminals there, and the total is the sum over all states.
Build the closure of the start state, then the states reached on each terminal. In each, list the complete items and the terminals standing right after a dot.
Start with $S' \to \bullet S$ and close it. Write the complete item that appears when $A$ is expanded to nothing, and list which terminals can be shifted in that same state.

variation.explanation: The state where $A \to \epsilon$ is complete beside the shift $A \to \bullet aA$ occurs twice: the start state and the state after reading $a$. Each gives one conflicting cell, on $a$. The states for $B$ hold only shifts or a single complete item, so they add nothing. Counting only the start state gives 1, and counting a conflict in each $B$ state wrongly gives 3 or 4. This is generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: For a grammar to be LL(1), it must be left-recursive
For a grammar to be LL(1), it must be left-factored
The LL(1) parsers are more powerful than the SLR parsers

steps.title: What LL(1) means
steps.body: An LL(1) parser reads the input from Left to right, builds a Leftmost derivation, and uses 1 token of lookahead. It is predictive: a table $M[A, t]$ tells it which production of nonterminal $A$ to use when the next token is $t$. A grammar is LL(1) exactly when no table cell holds two productions. For two alternatives $A \to \alpha \mid \beta$ this needs $\text{FIRST}(\alpha) \cap \text{FIRST}(\beta) = \emptyset$ (and, if one is nullable, the other's FIRST must avoid $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$).

steps.title: Test each statement against that rule
steps.body: (A) False. A predictive parser chooses the rule from the table and never retries, so it does no backtracking. (B) False. Left recursion $A \to A\alpha \mid \beta$ puts the same tokens in $\text{FIRST}(A\alpha)$ and $\text{FIRST}(\beta)$, so one cell holds two rules; an LL(1) grammar must have no left recursion. (C) True. If two alternatives share a prefix, such as $A \to ab \mid ac$, both start with the same token and the cell $M[A,a]$ holds two rules, so a common prefix has to be left-factored away. (D) False. LL(1) grammars generate only a proper part of the deterministic context-free languages, while the LR family (SLR, LALR, canonical LR) covers all of them. LL(1) is the weaker method.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (C) is true, which is the official key C.

shortcut.body: Memorise the three facts: LL(1) means no backtracking, no left recursion, no common prefix. Statements that reverse any of these ('requires left recursion', 'uses backtracking') are false at once. LL is weaker than LR, so any 'LL more powerful than LR/SLR' claim is false.

traps.text: Believing LL(1) backtracks. Recursive descent with backtracking exists, but the table-driven LL(1) parser chooses by one token and never backs up.
Reading 'must be left-recursive' as a property of grammars. It is the opposite: left recursion must be removed before a grammar can be LL(1).
Thinking top-down is stronger because it is simpler to write. In power, LR parsers handle every grammar class that LL(1) handles at the language level and many more.

recognize.clues: The four statements are about what makes a grammar LL(1): backtracking, left recursion, left factoring, and strength against SLR. Each is settled by the single rule that a table cell may hold only one production.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse LL(1) with recursive descent with backtracking, which can try alternatives that share a prefix. An LL(1) parser never retries, so a shared prefix has to be removed first.

check.body: Use a different route for the two grammar-shape claims. The grammar $S \to aS \mid b$ is left-factored and not left-recursive: FIRST of the alternatives is $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$, so each cell holds one rule and the string $aab$ parses by the table with no retry. The grammar $S \to Sa \mid b$ is left-recursive: $b$ is in FIRST of both alternatives, so $M[S,b]$ holds two rules, yet a shift-reduce parser reads $baa$ by reducing $b$ to $S$ and then $Sa$ to $S$ twice. That grammar is easy for LR and not LL(1), which is the direction of the power comparison.

hints.text: Test each statement against what a predictive parser needs. Which statements describe something an LL(1) grammar must have, and which something it must not have?
LL(1) reads Left to right, builds a Leftmost derivation, and looks 1 token ahead. The table cell $M[A,t]$ must name exactly one production, so the parser never guesses and never retries.
If two alternatives of one nonterminal can start with the same token, they land in the same cell. Ask which shapes of rule produce that overlap and what must be done to them.

Turn each statement into a claim about tokens. Backtracking means retrying a choice. Left recursion $A \to A\alpha$ gives $A$ the first tokens of $A$. A shared prefix gives two alternatives the same first token.
For the power comparison, ask which class of grammars each method accepts, and whether one class contains the other.

variation.stem: Which of the following statements about LL(1) grammars is/are true?
options: An LL(1) parser builds a rightmost derivation in reverse
Every LL(1) grammar can be parsed by a canonical LR(1) parser
A cell of an LL(1) table may hold two productions when the next token is $\$$
variation.explanation: A table cell holds one production, so each string has one leftmost derivation and one tree; an ambiguous grammar can never fill its table that way. LL(1) is a subset of LR(1), so a canonical LR(1) parser handles every LL(1) grammar. LL(1) builds a leftmost derivation, not a rightmost one, and a doubly filled cell is exactly what makes a grammar not LL(1). This is generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem: Given a Context-Free Grammar $G$ as follows: $S \to Aa \mid bAc \mid dc \mid bda$; $A \to d$. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

solutionDiagram.alt: The two states containing A to d where SLR sees a shift-reduce conflict but the LR(1) lookaheads a and c separate the actions

steps.title: Parsers compared, in plain words
steps.body: All LR parsers read left to right and build a rightmost derivation in reverse, using a state machine of items (a production with a dot, such as $A \to d\bullet$). They differ in when they allow a reduction. SLR(1) reduces $A \to \alpha\bullet$ whenever the next token is in $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$, the set of tokens that can follow $A$ anywhere in the grammar. Canonical LR(1) attaches to each item the exact tokens that may follow in that state's context. LALR(1) takes the LR(1) states and merges those that have the same items ignoring lookaheads. A conflict is a state where two actions are allowed on one token.

steps.title: FOLLOW(A) and the SLR conflicts
steps.body: $A$ appears in $S \to Aa$ (followed by $a$) and in $S \to bAc$ (followed by $c$), so $\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{a, c\}$. Consider the state reached by reading $d$ from the start: $\{S \to d\bullet c,\ A \to d\bullet\}$. SLR reduces on $a$ and $c$, but $S \to d\bullet c$ shifts $c$, so token $c$ is a shift-reduce conflict. Likewise the state after $b\,d$ is $\{A \to d\bullet,\ S \to bd\bullet a\}$, which reduces on $a$ and shifts $a$. So $G$ is not SLR(1).

steps.title: LR(1) lookaheads remove both conflicts
steps.body: In the first state, $A \to d\bullet$ comes from $S \to \bullet Aa$, so its only lookahead is $a$; the shift is on $c$. No overlap. In the state after $b\,d$, $A \to d\bullet$ comes from $S \to b\bullet Ac$, so its lookahead is $c$; the shift is on $a$. No overlap. The two states have different cores, so LALR merging joins nothing there.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: $G$ is LALR(1) but not SLR(1): option (C). Option (B) fails because LALR(1) has no conflict, and (D) fails because SLR(1) does.

shortcut.body: Find the single reduce that shares a state with a shift. Here it is $A \to d$ meeting $S \to d\bullet c$ and $S \to bd\bullet a$. If $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$ contains the shifted token, SLR fails ($\{a,c\}$ contains both $c$ and $a$). Then ask whether the lookahead differs by context; it does ($a$ versus $c$), so LR(1) succeeds, and with no merge possible LALR does too. Unsafe when two states share a core, since LALR merging could then add a reduce-reduce conflict.

traps.text: Concluding it is neither LALR nor SLR because the SLR conflicts exist. SLR is the weaker test; its failure says nothing about LR(1) or LALR(1).
Assuming LALR always loses power relative to canonical LR. It does only when merged states pick up a reduce-reduce conflict, and here no two states have equal cores.
Checking only that $A \to d$ is the sole reduction and calling it SLR. The state still holds a shift on a token in $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$.

recognize.clues: The stem asks to classify one grammar among CLR(1), LALR(1) and SLR(1). The rule $A \to d$ is reached in two contexts, one before $a$ and one before $c$, so FOLLOW (which pools contexts) must be compared with the per-state lookahead.
recognize.contrast: SLR(1) uses FOLLOW sets only. Do not stop there: an SLR conflict does not mean the grammar fails LALR(1) or LR(1), because the lookaheads can differ by context.

check.body: Count the canonical LR(1) states that hold a reducing item. The state after $d$ has core $\{S \to d\bullet c,\ A \to d\bullet\}$ and the state after $bd$ has core $\{A \to d\bullet,\ S \to bd\bullet a\}$. Each core occurs once, so LALR merging joins nothing and cannot add a conflict. Then parse the strings that use the reduce: on $da$ the state after $d$ sees $a$ and reduces $A \to d$, then shifts $a$ and reduces $S \to Aa$; on $bdc$ the state after $bd$ sees $c$ and reduces, then shifts $c$ and reduces $S \to bAc$. Each token picks one action.

hints.text: Rank the three parser classes from most to least permissive. Then look for the single state where the weakest of them first gets stuck.

SLR reduces on FOLLOW of the left side. Canonical LR(1) reduces only on the lookahead carried by the item in that exact state. LALR merges canonical states with the same core and unions their lookaheads.
A grammar fails SLR when FOLLOW of a reduced symbol contains a token that a shift in the same state uses. It fails LALR only if merging same-core states creates a conflict that was not there before.
Compute FOLLOW($A$) from the places $A$ occurs. Then build the state reached by reading $d$ first and the state reached by reading $b$ then $d$, and write out the items of each.

In the state after the first $d$, the reducing item $A \to d\bullet$ arrived from $S \to \bullet Aa$. Work out which single token can follow $A$ in that context and compare it with the shift in the same state.

variation.stem: Given the context-free grammar $G$: $S \to Aa \mid bAc \mid Bc \mid bBa$; $A \to d$; $B \to d$. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?
variation.explanation: After reading $d$ and after reading $bd$ there are states holding both $A \to d\bullet$ and $B \to d\bullet$. In the first the lookaheads are $a$ for $A$ and $c$ for $B$, in the second $c$ for $A$ and $a$ for $B$, so canonical LR(1) has no conflict. LALR merges these two states because their cores match, giving both reductions the lookaheads $\{a, c\}$ and a reduce-reduce conflict. SLR fails for the same reason. questions.stem: Consider two grammars $G_1$ and $G_2$ with the production rules given below: $G_1$: $S \to \text{if } E \text{ then } S \mid \text{if } E \text{ then } S \text{ else } S \mid a$; $E \to b$. $G_2$: $S \to \text{if } E \text{ then } S \mid M$; $M \to \text{if } E \text{ then } M \text{ else } S \mid c$; $E \to b$. Here $\text{if, then, else}, a, b, c$ are the terminals. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

solutionDiagram.alt: Two different parse trees for the same 14-token string in grammar G2, showing that G2 is ambiguous

steps.title: Two properties, defined
steps.body: A grammar is LL(1) if a single lookahead token always picks the production: for every nonterminal, the sets $\text{FIRST}$ of its alternatives must be disjoint. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two parse trees. 'Dangling else' is the classic ambiguity: in $\text{if } b \text{ then if } b \text{ then } a \text{ else } a$ the else could belong to either if.

steps.title: G1
steps.body: The first two alternatives of $S$ both begin with $\text{if}$, so $\text{FIRST}$ sets overlap and cell $M[S, \text{if}]$ holds two rules: $G_1$ is not LL(1). It is ambiguous: the else can attach to the inner if or to the outer if, giving two trees for $\text{if } b \text{ then if } b \text{ then } a \text{ else } a$.

steps.title: G2: not LL(1)
steps.body: $S \to \text{if } E \text{ then } S$ starts with $\text{if}$, and $S \to M$ can also start with $\text{if}$ because $M \to \text{if } E \text{ then } M \text{ else } S$. The two alternatives of $S$ share the lookahead $\text{if}$, so $G_2$ is not LL(1).

steps.title: G2: still ambiguous
steps.body: $G_2$ looks like the standard fix (an else only after a matched $M$), but the else branch of $M$ is $S$, not $M$. Take $\text{if } b \text{ then if } b \text{ then } c \text{ else if } b \text{ then } c \text{ else } c$ (14 tokens). In tree 1 (root $S \to \text{if } E \text{ then } S$) the first if has no else, the second if takes the first else and the third if takes the last else. In tree 2 (root $S \to M$) the first if takes the last else, and the second if takes the first else, whose else branch is the short $\text{if } b \text{ then } c$. Both are valid, as the drawing shows.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: $G_1$ and $G_2$ are both not LL(1) and both ambiguous. (A) and (B) are false; (C) and (D) are true: official key C;D.

shortcut.body: Check LL(1) by writing the $\text{FIRST}$ of $S$'s alternatives: two of them start with $\text{if}$ in each grammar, so (A) and (B) die at once, leaving (C) and (D). Then ask whether the textbook matched-else fix is exact: the else part of $M$ must be $M$ again ($M \to \text{if } E \text{ then } M \text{ else } M$). Here it is $S$, so the fix is broken and (D) holds.

traps.text: Treating $G_2$ as the unambiguous, parseable fix. Only the else-closes-a-matched-if idea is borrowed; the else side being $S$ reopens the ambiguity, and the shared $\text{if}$ prefix keeps it out of LL(1).
Thinking $G_1$ is LL(1) because one extra token of lookahead (the one after the condition) could tell the alternatives apart. LL(1) has one token, and the left-factoring needed is not present.
Stopping after proving (C) and leaving out (D). Candidates assume $G_2$ is unambiguous and do not test the long string with two else parts.
Leaving out (D) because only $G_1$ shows the textbook dangling else. $G_2$'s ambiguity needs two elses and three ifs.

recognize.clues: Two if-then-else grammars are given: the plain dangling-else form and a matched/unmatched repair. The options combine LL(1) status with ambiguity, so both the FIRST-overlap test and a two-trees search are needed.
recognize.contrast: An ambiguous grammar is never LL(1), but a grammar that fails the LL(1) test is not thereby ambiguous. Use the FIRST-overlap test for the LL(1) options and a witness string for the ambiguity options.

check.body: Count parse trees mechanically. For $G_1$ the string $\text{if } b \text{ then if } b \text{ then } a \text{ else } a$ has 2 trees. For $G_2$ the string $\text{if } b \text{ then if } b \text{ then } c \text{ else if } b \text{ then } c \text{ else } c$ also has 2 trees. In the FIRST test both grammars give $\text{if}$ for two alternatives of $S$, so each fills one cell twice.

hints.text: Two separate properties are in play: whether one token of lookahead picks the production, and whether some string has two parse trees. One of them may settle two options by itself.
LL(1) needs the FIRST sets of a nonterminal's alternatives to be disjoint. Ambiguity means one string with two trees, and the dangling else is the standard example.
When two alternatives of one nonterminal can begin with the same token, the table cell is filled twice and the grammar is not LL(1). That test needs only the first tokens of each alternative.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE while computing First and Follow during top down parsing by a compiler?
options: For a production $A \to \epsilon$, $\epsilon$ will be added to $First(A)$.
If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to $First(S)$, where $S$ is the start symbol.
For a production $A \to \epsilon$, $\epsilon$ will be added to $Follow(A)$.
If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to $Follow(S)$, where $S$ is the start symbol.

steps.title: FIRST, FOLLOW and the markers, defined
steps.body: $\text{FIRST}(X)$ is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from $X$, plus $\epsilon$ (the empty string) when $X$ can derive nothing. $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$ is the set of terminals that can appear immediately after $A$ in some sentential form, plus the end marker $\$$ when $A$ can end the input. Two facts decide this question: $\epsilon$ belongs only to FIRST (it records that a symbol can vanish), and $\$$ belongs only to FOLLOW (it marks where the input ends and is not part of any derived string).

steps.title: Check the four statements
steps.body: (A) True. For $A \to \epsilon$, $A$ derives the empty string, so $\epsilon \in \text{FIRST}(A)$. (B) False. $\$$ is not a terminal that begins any string, so it never enters a FIRST set. (C) False. FOLLOW contains terminals and $\$$ only; $\epsilon$ is never put in a FOLLOW set. (D) True. The start symbol is followed by the end marker, so $\$ \in \text{FOLLOW}(S)$ is the initial rule of the FOLLOW algorithm.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: (A) and (D), official key A;D.

shortcut.body: Remember the placement: $\epsilon$ lives in FIRST only, $\$$ lives in FOLLOW only, and FOLLOW of the start symbol begins as $\{\$\}$. Any statement that puts them in the other set is false.

traps.text: Putting $\$$ into $\text{FIRST}(S)$ because it is the 'right end marker' of the input. FIRST describes how derived strings begin; the end marker only ever follows.
Adding $\epsilon$ to $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$ for $A \to \epsilon$. The empty rule affects FIRST (and the rule for passing FOLLOW along), never puts $\epsilon$ in FOLLOW.

recognize.clues: The question is a statement test, not a computation. It asks where $\epsilon$ and the end marker $\$$ may appear, which are the two special symbols in the definitions of FIRST and FOLLOW.
recognize.contrast: FIRST and FOLLOW are easy to swap: $\epsilon$ lives only in FIRST and $\$$ only in FOLLOW. A nullable rule puts $\epsilon$ into FIRST of its left side, never into FOLLOW.

check.body: Test on the grammar $S \to aA$, $A \to \epsilon$. Here FIRST($A$) is $\{\epsilon\}$, and FOLLOW($A$) equals FOLLOW($S$), which is $\{\$\}$. The LL(1) table then puts $A \to \epsilon$ in the column for $\$$, so the end marker is used in FOLLOW and never needs $\epsilon$ there.

questions.stem: Consider the following context-free grammar where the start symbol is $S$ and the set of terminals is $\{a,b,c,d\}$: $S \to AaAb \mid BbBa$; $A \to cS \mid \epsilon$; $B \to dS \mid \epsilon$. The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table. Which one of the following options represents the CORRECT combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table? Note: In the options, "blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty.

solutionDiagram.alt: The completed LL(1) table with cells (1) to (4) filled from the FIRST and FOLLOW sets

steps.title: How an LL(1) table is filled
steps.body: Cell $M[X, t]$ names the production to use when nonterminal $X$ is on top and the next token is $t$. For a production $X \to \alpha$: put it in column $t$ for every $t \in \text{FIRST}(\alpha)$; and if $\alpha$ can derive the empty string, also put it in column $t$ for every $t \in \text{FOLLOW}(X)$. $\text{FIRST}$ lists the tokens a string can start with; $\text{FOLLOW}(X)$ lists the tokens that can come right after $X$.

steps.title: Compute the sets
steps.body: $\text{FIRST}(A) = \{c, \epsilon\}$, $\text{FIRST}(B) = \{d, \epsilon\}$. For $AaAb$, $A$ may vanish and then $a$ appears, so $\text{FIRST}(AaAb) = \{c, a\}$; likewise $\text{FIRST}(BbBa) = \{d, b\}$. $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$: in $AaAb$ the first $A$ is followed by $a$ and the second by $b$, so $\{a, b\}$. $\text{FOLLOW}(B) = \{a, b\}$ in the same way.

steps.title: Fill the four numbered cells
steps.body: (1) $M[S, c]$: $c \in \text{FIRST}(AaAb)$, so $S \to AaAb$. (2) $M[S, d]$: $d \in \text{FIRST}(BbBa)$, so $S \to BbBa$. (3) $M[A, b]$: $A \to \epsilon$ is used for $\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{a, b\}$, so $b$ gets $A \to \epsilon$ (matching the $a$ cell already shown). (4) $M[B, a]$: $B \to \epsilon$ for $\text{FOLLOW}(B) = \{a,b\}$, so $a$ gets $B \to \epsilon$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: (1) $S \to AaAb$, (2) $S \to BbBa$, (3) $A \to \epsilon$, (4) $B \to \epsilon$: option (A).

shortcut.body: Two eliminations. The table already shows $A \to \epsilon$ under $a$; because $\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{a,b\}$ contains $b$ too, cell (3) cannot be blank, which kills (C) and (D). Then $c$ starts only through $A$, so (1) is the $A$-rule $S \to AaAb$, which kills (B).

traps.text: Swapping (1) and (2): taking $c$ as the start of the $B$-rule. $c$ begins only through $A \to cS$, so it belongs to $S \to AaAb$.
Leaving (3) and (4) blank, forgetting that nullable rules go in the FOLLOW columns. $b$ follows $A$ and $a$ follows $B$.
Both errors together: swapped productions and blank cells.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a partly filled LL(1) table and asks which cells are filled or blank. The grammar has two nullable nonterminals, so cells come from FIRST of the right side and also from FOLLOW of the left side.
recognize.contrast: Do not fill cells from FIRST alone. The cells of an $\epsilon$-rule depend on FOLLOW, and dropping that part leaves the cells blank when they should hold $\epsilon$.

check.body: Parse two strings of the language by the table. The string $ab$ comes from $S \to AaAb$ with both $A$ empty: after matching $a$ the parser has $A$ on top with next token $b$, and needs cell (3) to hold $A \to \epsilon$. The string $ba$ comes from $S \to BbBa$: after $b$ the parser has $B$ on top with next token $a$, and needs cell (4) to hold $B \to \epsilon$. A blank in either cell would reject a valid string.

questions.stem: Consider the following augmented grammar, which is to be parsed with a SLR parser. The set of terminals is $\{a, b, c, d, \#, @\}$: $S' \to S$; $S \to SS \mid Aa \mid bAc \mid Bc \mid bBa$; $A \to d\#$; $B \to @$. Let $I_0 = \text{CLOSURE}(\{S' \to \bullet S\})$. The number of items in the set $\text{GOTO}(I_0, S)$ is ___________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Kernel items S prime to S dot and S to S dot S plus the 7 closure items give 9 items in GOTO(I0, S)

steps.title: Items, closure and GOTO
steps.body: An item is a production with a dot showing how much has been read, such as $S \to S\bullet S$. CLOSURE adds more items: whenever the dot stands before a nonterminal $N$, add $N \to \bullet\gamma$ for every rule of $N$, and repeat for the new items. $\text{GOTO}(I, X)$ moves the dot over $X$ in every item of $I$ that has $X$ right after the dot, then takes the closure of those items. Count the items in the finished set.

steps.title: Move the dot over S
steps.body: $I_0$ holds $S' \to \bullet S$ and, after closure, all five $S$-rules with the dot first, plus $A \to \bullet d\#$ and $B \to \bullet @$. Items with $S$ right after the dot: $S' \to \bullet S$ and $S \to \bullet SS$. Moving the dot gives the kernel $\{S' \to S\bullet,\ S \to S\bullet S\}$, 2 items.

steps.title: Close the kernel
steps.body: $S \to S\bullet S$ has the dot before $S$, so add the five $S$-rules: $S \to \bullet SS$, $S \to \bullet Aa$, $S \to \bullet bAc$, $S \to \bullet Bc$, $S \to \bullet bBa$ (5 items). Those put the dot before $A$ and $B$, so add $A \to \bullet d\#$ and $B \to \bullet @$ (2 items). Nothing else starts with a nonterminal after the dot. That gives $2 + 5 + 2 = 9$ items.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: $\text{GOTO}(I_0, S)$ has 9 items.

shortcut.body: Count the rules of the grammar with the dot at the front: five $S$-rules, one $A$-rule, one $B$-rule = 7. Add the two kernel items $S' \to S\bullet$ and $S \to S\bullet S$, giving 9. This works because the dot in $S \to S\bullet S$ is before $S$, which pulls in every $S$-rule, and in turn $A$ and $B$. It is unsafe if the dot lands before a terminal, which would add nothing.

traps.text: Answering 2: counting only the kernel items and forgetting the closure.
Answering 7 or 8: dropping the two kernel items, or leaving out $S \to \bullet SS$ because it looks like a duplicate of the item you came from. It is a new item in the closure.
Answering 10 or more: counting $S' \to \bullet S$ again. After the dot moves over $S$ that item is gone.

recognize.clues: The stem names CLOSURE and GOTO and asks for the number of items in a set. The left-recursive rule $S \to SS$ means the dot meets $S$ again after the move, which pulls in all the $S$-rules and then $A$ and $B$.
recognize.contrast: The stem says SLR parser, but SLR builds the same LR(0) item sets and differs only in how the table is filled with FOLLOW. No FOLLOW computation is needed to count items.

check.body: Recount from $I_0$. It holds $S' \to \bullet S$, five $S$-rules, $A \to \bullet d\#$ and $B \to \bullet @$, which is 8 items. $\text{GOTO}(I_0, S)$ drops $S' \to \bullet S$ and gains the two kernel items $S' \to S\bullet$ and $S \to S\bullet S$, while the closure items stay the same. That is $8 - 1 + 2$ $= 9$, the same as the $2 + 5 + 2$ count.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are Bottom-Up Parser(s)?

steps.title: Top-down versus bottom-up
steps.body: A parser turns a token string into a parse tree. A top-down parser starts from the start symbol and expands nonterminals to match the input, building a leftmost derivation; recursive descent, predictive and LL(1) parsers are of this type. A bottom-up parser starts from the tokens and repeatedly replaces a right-hand side by its left-hand side, finishing at the start symbol; it builds a rightmost derivation in reverse. Shift-reduce is the general bottom-up scheme (shift a token onto a stack, reduce the top of the stack by a rule), and LR parsers (LR(0), SLR, LALR, canonical LR) are its table-driven forms.

steps.title: Classify the four
steps.body: (A) Shift-reduce parser: bottom-up. (B) Predictive parser: top-down, it predicts the production from the lookahead. (C) LL(1) parser: top-down. (D) LR parser: bottom-up. So the bottom-up parsers are (A) and (D).

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: (A) and (D), official key A;D.

shortcut.body: Letters tell the direction: LL, predictive and recursive descent are top-down; LR and shift-reduce are bottom-up. Under 20 seconds.

traps.text: Picking 'predictive' because it sounds table-driven like LR. A predictive parser expands from the start symbol, so it is top-down.
Picking LL(1) as bottom-up since it reads input left to right. The first L is the scan direction; the second L says the derivation is leftmost, which is top-down.

recognize.clues: The stem asks which named parsers work bottom-up. Names to sort are shift-reduce, predictive, LL(1) and LR, so the direction of each family decides the answer.
recognize.contrast: Predictive and LL(1) parsers also read left to right but build a leftmost derivation from the start symbol. Same input order, opposite direction of tree building.

check.body: Test each name by the move it makes. If it guesses a production from the lookahead before reading the tokens it covers, it is top-down. If it pushes tokens and then replaces a matched right-hand side by its left-hand side, it is bottom-up.

questions.stem: Consider the operator precedence and associativity rules for the integer arithmetic operators given in the table below. The value of the expression $3 + 1 + 5 * 2 / 7 + 2 - 4 - 7 - 6 / 2$ as per the above rules is __________

solutionDiagram.alt: The expression collapsed in four stages: plus runs first, then the minus run grouped to the right, then star, then slash, ending at 6

steps.title: Precedence and associativity, defined
steps.body: Precedence says which operator is applied first when different operators meet: higher precedence binds tighter, like brackets around it. Associativity says how to group a run of operators of the same precedence: left means $a \circ b \circ c = (a \circ b) \circ c$, right means $a \circ (b \circ c)$. Here the order from tightest to loosest is $+$, then $-$, then $*$, then $/$, which is unlike ordinary arithmetic. Division is integer division.

steps.title: Apply $+$ first (highest, left)
steps.body: The runs of $+$ are $3+1+5$ and $7+2$ (the operands around the $+$ signs). Left to right: $3+1+5 = 9$ and $7+2 = 9$. The expression becomes $9 * 2 / 9 - 4 - 7 - 6 / 2$.

steps.title: Apply $-$ next (right-associative)
steps.body: The minus run is $9 - 4 - 7 - 6$ (the first operand is the result 9 from $7+2$). Right grouping: $9 - (4 - (7 - 6)) = 9 - (4 - 1) = 9 - 3 = 6$. The expression becomes $9 * 2 / 6 / 2$.

steps.title: Then $*$, then $/$
steps.body: $*$ is next: $9 * 2 = 18$, leaving $18 / 6 / 2$. Division is right-associative: $18 / (6 / 2) = 18 / 3 = 6$.

shortcut.body: Write the expression with the operands numbered and collapse operators strictly in the order $+, -, *, /$, grouping each run in its stated direction. Do not fall back on habit: reading it with the usual rules gives $-7$, which is a different number.

traps.text: Using usual arithmetic precedence ($*$ and $/$ before $+$ and $-$, all left-associative) gives $-7$.
Evaluating strictly left to right with no precedence gives $-6$ (integer division truncated).
Grouping the minus run to the left, $((9-4)-7)-6 = -8$, instead of to the right, changes the quotient to $18 / (-8/2) = -4$ and misses 6.

recognize.clues: A table gives an unusual precedence order and a direction of grouping for each of four operators, then asks for a numeric value. The task is to follow the given rules, not the school ones.
recognize.contrast: This is evaluation under stated rules, not ambiguity of a grammar. The table settles the grouping, so every expression has one tree.

check.body: Parse from the loosest operator down instead of evaluating from the tightest. Split at the two $/$ signs, grouped to the right: $(3+1+5*2)\ /\ ((7+2-4-7-6)\ /\ 2)$. The left part is $(3+1+5)*2 = 18$. In the right part, $7+2 = 9$ and the minus run $9-4-7-6$ groups to the right as $9-(4-(7-6)) = 6$, so the part is $6/2 = 3$. Then $18/3 = 6$, the same value from the opposite order of work.

questions.stem: Consider the following grammar $G$, with $S$ as the start symbol. The grammar $G$ has three incomplete productions denoted by (1), (2), and (3): $S \to daT \mid (1)$; $T \to aS \mid bT \mid (2)$; $R \to (3) \mid \epsilon$. The set of terminals is $\{a,b,c,d,f\}$. The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different non-terminals are as follows. $\text{FIRST}(S) = \{c,d,f\}$, $\text{FIRST}(T) = \{a,b,\epsilon\}$, $\text{FIRST}(R) = \{c,\epsilon\}$; $\text{FOLLOW}(S) = \text{FOLLOW}(T) = \{c,f,\$\}$, $\text{FOLLOW}(R) = \{f\}$. Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete productions?

steps.title: What FIRST and FOLLOW say
steps.body: $\text{FIRST}(X)$ is the set of terminals that can start a string derived from $X$, with $\epsilon$ when $X$ can derive the empty string. $\text{FOLLOW}(X)$ is the set of terminals that can come right after $X$, with $\$$ if $X$ can end the input. We are given both sets and must pick the productions that reproduce them. Each given set is a constraint to test.

steps.title: Fill in (2) from $T$
steps.body: $\text{FIRST}(T)$ contains $\epsilon$, but $T \to aS$ and $T \to bT$ cannot derive the empty string, so (2) must be $T \to \epsilon$. The alternative $T \to cT$ would put $c$ into $\text{FIRST}(T)$, which is not allowed. This rules out options (C) and (D).

steps.title: Fill in (1) from $S$
steps.body: $\text{FIRST}(S) = \{c, d, f\}$. The rule $S \to daT$ gives only $d$. The missing $c$ and $f$ must come from (1). With (1) $= Rf$ and $R$ nullable: $\text{FIRST}(Rf) = (\text{FIRST}(R) \setminus \{\epsilon\}) \cup \{f\} = \{c, f\}$, so $\text{FIRST}(S) = \{c,d,f\}$ as given. With (1) $= fR$ only $f$ is added and $c$ is missing, so $S \to fR$ fails. That rules out (B).

steps.title: Check (3) and FOLLOW
steps.body: With $S \to Rf$, $\text{FOLLOW}(R)$ contains $f$, matching $\{f\}$, and $R \to cTR$ gives $\text{FIRST}(R) = \{c, \epsilon\}$ as given. In $R \to cTR$, $T$ is followed by $\text{FIRST}(R)\setminus\{\epsilon\} = \{c\}$ plus $\text{FOLLOW}(R) = \{f\}$ because $R$ is nullable, and $T \to aS$ gives $\text{FOLLOW}(T) \supseteq \text{FOLLOW}(S)$; with $\$$ coming from the start symbol this gives $\{c, f, \$\}$ for both. Checking all four options against the given sets, only option (A) reproduces them.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: (1) $S \to Rf$, (2) $T \to \epsilon$, (3) $R \to cTR$: option (A).

shortcut.body: Two quick kills. $\text{FIRST}(T)$ holds $\epsilon$, so (2) must be $\epsilon$-deriving: options with $T \to cT$ ((C), (D)) fail. $S \to fR$ gives $\text{FIRST}(S)$ only $f$ and $d$, never $c$: options with $S \to fR$ fail, leaving (A).

traps.text: Choosing $S \to fR$: it looks natural with $f$ in FOLLOW$(R)$, but then $c$ is missing from $\text{FIRST}(S)$ and $f$ no longer follows $R$.
Choosing $T \to cT$, which adds $c$ to $\text{FIRST}(T)$ and removes $\epsilon$ from it; both disagree with the given set.
Combining $S \to Rf$ with $T \to cT$ and $R \to cR$: the $S$ part is right, but $\text{FIRST}(T)$ is wrong and $\text{FOLLOW}(T)$ comes out as $\{\$\}$ instead of $\{c,f,\$\}$.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The LALR (1) parser for a grammar G cannot have reduce-reduce conflict if the LR (1) parser for G does not have reduce-reduce conflict.
Symbol table is accessed only during the lexical analysis phase.
Data flow analysis is necessary for run-time memory management.
LR (1) parsing is sufficient for deterministic context-free languages.

steps.title: Terms used by the four statements
steps.body: LR(1) parsing builds states of items, each carrying one exact lookahead token. LALR(1) merges all LR(1) states that have the same items when lookaheads are ignored (the same core), which shrinks the table. A reduce-reduce conflict is a state where two different rules are complete on the same lookahead. The symbol table stores each name with its type and scope. Data flow analysis is a compile-time study of how values move through a program.

steps.title: Judge each statement
steps.body: (A) False. Merging LR(1) states can union lookaheads of two different reductions and create a reduce-reduce conflict that LR(1) did not have. Example: $S \to aAd \mid bBd \mid aBe \mid bAe$, $A \to c$, $B \to c$ is conflict-free in LR(1) (14 states) but the merged LALR(1) automaton (13 states) has a reduce-reduce conflict in the merged state, on $d$ and on $e$. Merging never creates a shift-reduce conflict, only reduce-reduce. (B) False. The symbol table is used by the semantic analyser, the intermediate-code generator and the code generator as well, not only by the lexer. (C) False. Run-time memory management is about stacks and heaps and activation records; data flow analysis serves optimisation. (D) True. Every deterministic context-free language has an LR(1) grammar, and an LR(1) parser accepts it, so LR(1) is sufficient for the whole class.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Statement (D) is the true one, so the answer is option (D), matching the official key.

shortcut.body: Eliminate by phase facts: the symbol table is used across many phases (B), data flow is for optimisation, not run-time memory (C), and LALR can introduce reduce-reduce conflicts (A). What is left is the textbook theorem that LR(1) covers all DCFLs.

traps.text: Believing LALR merging is harmless because the table is built from LR(1). Merged lookahead sets can overlap and create a reduce-reduce conflict.
Thinking the symbol table is only the lexer's job because names are first seen there. Later phases read and update it for types and scopes.
Confusing optimisation with storage allocation. Data flow analysis does not manage run-time memory.

recognize.clues: Four general statements about parser classes and compiler phases, one of which is true. The words LALR(1), LR(1) and deterministic context-free languages place it in the parser hierarchy.
recognize.contrast: Statement (A) tempts you to treat LALR(1) merging as harmless. Merging same-core states can union lookaheads and add reduce-reduce conflicts, though never shift-reduce ones, so look for which conflict merging can add.

check.body: Verify the refutation of (A) by hand on $S \to aAd \mid bBd \mid aBe \mid bAe$, $A \to c$, $B \to c$. After $ac$ the LR(1) state holds $[A \to c\bullet, d]$ and $[B \to c\bullet, e]$; after $bc$ it holds $[B \to c\bullet, d]$ and $[A \to c\bullet, e]$. Each lookahead picks one reduction, so LR(1) has no conflict. The two states share a core, and merging gives $A \to c\bullet$ and $B \to c\bullet$ both on $\{d, e\}$, a reduce-reduce conflict. So (A) is false.

questions.stem: Consider the augmented grammar with $\{+, *, (, ), id\}$ as the set of terminals. $S' \to S$; $S \to S + R \mid R$; $R \to R * P \mid P$; $P \to (S) \mid id$. If $I_0$ is the set of two $LR(0)$ items $\{[S' \to S\bullet],\ [S \to S\bullet + R]\}$, then $goto(closure(I_0), +)$ contains exactly __________ items.

solutionDiagram.alt: Moving the dot over plus from S to S dot plus R gives S to S plus dot R with R and P closure items, five in total

steps.title: Items, closure and goto, defined
steps.body: An LR(0) item is a rule with a dot showing how much has been read, such as $S \to S\bullet + R$. $\text{closure}(I)$ adds items: if the dot stands before a nonterminal, add every rule of that nonterminal with the dot at the front, and repeat. $\text{goto}(I, X)$ takes the items whose dot is right before $X$, moves the dot past $X$, and takes the closure. The question is the size of the resulting set.

steps.title: closure of $I_0$ adds nothing
steps.body: In $S' \to S\bullet$ the dot is at the end, and in $S \to S\bullet + R$ the dot is before the terminal $+$. Neither has a nonterminal after the dot, so $\text{closure}(I_0) = I_0$.

steps.title: goto on $+$
steps.body: Only $S \to S\bullet + R$ has $+$ after the dot. Moving the dot gives $S \to S + \bullet R$. The dot is now before $R$, so add $R \to \bullet R * P$ and $R \to \bullet P$. The second of these has the dot before $P$, so add $P \to \bullet (S)$ and $P \to \bullet id$. The new $R \to \bullet R*P$ has the dot before $R$, already present. Nothing more is added.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: $S \to S+\bullet R$, $R \to \bullet R*P$, $R \to \bullet P$, $P \to \bullet(S)$, $P \to \bullet id$: 5 items.

shortcut.body: Kernel is one item. The dot then sits before $R$, which has two rules, and the second rule's first symbol $P$ has two more: $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$. Count the rules of the nonterminals the closure reaches.

traps.text: Answering 1: forgetting closure after moving the dot.
Answering 3: adding the two $R$-rules but stopping before expanding $P$, which the rule $R \to \bullet P$ requires.
Answering 7 or 8: also including the $S$-rules or $S' \to \bullet S$ from the full start state; the dot is never before $S$ here.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a set of LR(0) items and asks how many items $goto(closure(I_0), +)$ contains. The words closure, goto and dot are the signature of building the LR(0) automaton.
recognize.contrast: Closure and goto are not FIRST and FOLLOW. They count items in an automaton state and do not look at lookahead.

check.body: Test that the set is closed. The symbols right after the dots in the five items are $R$, $R$, $P$, $($ and $id$. Both $R$ and $P$ already have all their rules present with the dot first, and no item has a dot before $S$, so closure can add nothing more and no $S$-rule belongs in the set. The five items are the kernel plus two rules of $R$ and two of $P$.

questions.stem: Consider the following ANSI C program (shown below). Which one of the following phases in a seven-phase C compiler will throw an error?

steps.title: The phases and what each one checks
steps.body: A compiler works in phases. The lexical analyser splits characters into tokens (identifiers, keywords, numbers) and complains only about characters or token shapes that no token can have. The syntax analyser checks that the tokens fit the grammar, for instance a declaration shaped as 'type name ;'. The semantic analyser checks meaning: names are declared before use, types match. Later phases (intermediate code, machine-independent optimiser, code generator, machine-dependent optimiser) only run on a program that passed these three.

steps.title: Walk the program through the phases
steps.body: The text is `Integer x;`. Lexical: `Integer` is not a C keyword (the keyword is `int`), so it is read as an ordinary identifier, and `x` and `;` are valid tokens. No lexical error. Syntax: the shape 'identifier identifier ;' matches a declaration where a type name is expected, and the grammar sees only that a name stands in the type position, so there is no syntax error. Semantic: the analyser looks the name `Integer` up in the symbol table, finds no type with that name, and reports an undeclared or unknown type error.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The error comes from the semantic analyser: option (C). The machine-dependent optimiser is never reached.

shortcut.body: Ask what kind of mistake it is. Nothing is misspelt as a token and nothing breaks the shape of a declaration; the only flaw is that the type name does not exist, a fact only the symbol table knows. Unknown names and type mismatches are semantic errors.

traps.text: Calling `Integer` an illegal token. Integer is a legal identifier token, so the lexer accepts it.
Treating the wrong keyword as a grammar error. The grammar matches a name in the type position, and whether that name is a type is decided later.
Picking the last phase on the list; an error stops compilation long before machine-dependent optimisation.

recognize.clues: A short C program with a type name that is not in C, and a question about which phase of a seven-phase compiler reports it. The program has a valid statement shape and a faulty name.
recognize.contrast: A syntax error breaks the grammar, for example a missing semicolon. An unknown type name keeps the shape and only breaks meaning.

check.body: Change one thing at a time. Replace `Integer` with `int` and the program becomes valid, so the fault is the name alone. A missing semicolon in the same line would instead break the grammar and be reported by the parser, which shows the difference between the two phases.

questions.stem: Consider the following augmented grammar with $\{\#, @, <, >, a, b, c\}$ as the set of terminals. $S' \to S$; $S \to S\#cS$; $S \to SS$; $S \to S@$; $S \to <S>$; $S \to a$; $S \to b$; $S \to c$. Let $I_0 = \text{CLOSURE}(\{S' \to \bullet S\})$. The number of items in the set $\text{GOTO}(\text{GOTO}(I_0, <), <)$ is __________

solutionDiagram.alt: Reading the bracket from the start state and again from the next state reaches the same eight-item set

steps.title: Items, closure and GOTO, defined
steps.body: An item is a rule with a dot marking progress. $\text{CLOSURE}$ adds, for every dot standing before a nonterminal, all rules of that nonterminal with the dot first, and repeats. $\text{GOTO}(I, X)$ moves the dot over $X$ in each item of $I$ that has $X$ right after the dot, then closes the result. We apply GOTO on the terminal $<$ twice.

steps.title: First GOTO on $<$
steps.body: In $I_0$ the only item with $<$ after the dot is $S \to \bullet <S>$. Moving it gives $S \to <\bullet S>$. The dot is before $S$, so closure adds every $S$-rule with the dot first: $S \to \bullet S\#cS$, $S \to \bullet SS$, $S \to \bullet S@$, $S \to \bullet <S>$, $S \to \bullet a$, $S \to \bullet b$, $S \to \bullet c$ (7 items). So $I_1$ has $1 + 7 = 8$ items.

steps.title: Second GOTO on $<$
steps.body: In $I_1$ the items with $<$ after the dot are again only $S \to \bullet <S>$ (the item $S \to <\bullet S>$ has $S$ after its dot). Moving it gives $S \to <\bullet S>$ and the same closure, so $\text{GOTO}(I_1, <) = I_1$: the machine loops back to the same state on $<$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: 1 kernel item plus 7 closure items is 8.

shortcut.body: Two $<$ in a row is a trick: the state after one $<$ already shows $S \to \bullet<S>$, so another $<$ reaches the same state. Count that state: kernel $S \to <\bullet S>$ plus all 7 $S$-rules = 8. Safe here because every $S$-rule is present in the closure.

traps.text: Answering 1: stopping after moving the dot and forgetting the closure.
Answering 7: counting only the closure and omitting the kernel item $S \to <\bullet S>$, or leaving out $S \to \bullet <S>$.
Answering 9 or more: including $S' \to \bullet S$, which belongs only to $I_0$.

recognize.clues: The stem applies GOTO twice on the same terminal to a closed state of an augmented grammar and asks for an item count. Closure, GOTO and dots mark the LR(0) automaton.
recognize.contrast: This is not an SLR table question: no lookaheads or FOLLOW sets are involved, only the items in a state.

check.body: Test the loop claim. A state is fixed by its kernel, and every state that contains $S \to \bullet <S>$ moves on $<$ to the kernel $S \to <\bullet S>$. So one, two or three moves on $<$ all land in the same state, which is why the count does not grow with the number of moves. That state is the kernel plus the 7 rules of $S$ ($S\#cS$, $SS$, $S@$, $<S>$, $a$, $b$, $c$), and the augmenting rule cannot enter, which gives 8.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements. $S_1$: Every SLR(1) grammar is unambiguous but there are certain unambiguous grammars that are not SLR(1). $S_2$: For any context-free grammar, there is a parser that takes at most $O(n^3)$ time to parse a string of length $n$. Which one of the following options is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Nested boxes: LR(0) inside SLR(1) inside LALR(1) inside LR(1) inside unambiguous grammars inside all context-free grammars, with the L = R grammar marked as unambiguous but outside SLR(1)

steps.title: The terms, and what each statement needs
steps.body: A grammar is ambiguous when some string has two different parse trees. A grammar is SLR(1) when the parser built from its LR(0) automaton, using one token of lookahead and the FOLLOW sets to decide reductions, never has a table cell with two actions (a conflict, such as shift against reduce). $n$ is the number of tokens in the input and $O(n^3)$ means the running time grows no faster than a constant times $n^3$. $S_1$ is an 'and' of two claims (SLR(1) implies unambiguous; some unambiguous grammar is not SLR(1)), so both must hold. $S_2$ asks for one parser that works for every context-free grammar in cubic time.

steps.title: First half of S1: SLR(1) implies unambiguous
steps.body: A conflict-free table makes the parser deterministic: for a given input there is exactly one sequence of shifts and reductions. The reductions, read backwards, are a rightmost derivation (that is what an LR parser builds), and every parse tree corresponds to its own rightmost derivation. Two parse trees would therefore need two different action sequences, which a conflict-free table cannot produce. So no SLR(1) grammar is ambiguous. A script tested this on 1509 random conflict-free grammars: none had a string with two parse trees up to length 6.

steps.title: Second half of S1: an unambiguous grammar that is not SLR(1)
steps.body: Take the pointer-assignment grammar $S \to L = R \mid R$, $L \to {*}R \mid \mathrm{id}$, $R \to L$. A script counted parse trees for every string up to 7 tokens and found at most one, so it is unambiguous. After reading a $L$ at the start of a statement the SLR automaton sits in a state holding both $S \to L \bullet = R$ and $R \to L \bullet$. The token $=$ is in $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(R)$ (because $L$ can be followed by $=$ and $L \to {*}R$ ends in $R$), so SLR(1) both shifts $=$ and reduces by $R \to L$: one conflict. Canonical LR(1) keeps the exact lookahead ($\$$ only) on the reduction and has no conflict. So $S_1$ is true.

steps.title: S2: any context-free grammar parses in cubic time
steps.body: Convert the grammar to Chomsky normal form (every rule is $A \to BC$ or $A \to a$), which keeps the language. The CYK algorithm fills a table with the nonterminals that derive each substring: there are about $n^2/2$ substrings, and for each one it tries every split point, at most $n$ of them, checking a fixed number of rules. For the worst case the number of split checks is exactly the sum below, and a script measured 10660 checks for $n = 40$, matching the formula. Earley's algorithm also gives $O(n^3)$ for every context-free grammar. So $S_2$ is true.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both statements are true, which is option (C).

shortcut.body: $S_2$ is the textbook fact that CYK and Earley parse any context-free grammar in cubic time, so it is true, which kills (A) and (D). Between (B) and (C) only $S_1$ matters: 'LR(1) grammars are unambiguous and SLR(1) sits inside LR(1)' is the standard theorem, and the pointer grammar $L = R$ is the standard unambiguous grammar that SLR(1) rejects. Safe, because both facts are standard textbook theorems.

traps.text: Believing $S_2$ is false because 'general parsing is exponential' (naive backtracking is). A table-driven algorithm such as CYK or Earley is cubic, so a cubic parser exists for every context-free grammar.

Believing $S_1$ is false, either by thinking an SLR(1) grammar can be ambiguous or by assuming every unambiguous grammar is SLR(1). The first is impossible (a conflict-free table gives one parse); the second fails for $S \to L = R \mid R$.
Rejecting both statements. $S_1$ is the standard SLR(1) fact and $S_2$ is the CYK bound, so neither can be false.

recognize.clues: Two statements about grammar classes. $S_1$ compares SLR(1) with ambiguity, so it sits in the parser hierarchy. $S_2$ is a time bound for parsing any context-free grammar, which points at the general table-filling parsers (CYK, Earley) rather than at a deterministic class.
recognize.contrast: Unambiguous is a property of a grammar, while LR(1) is a property of what a parser can decide. An unambiguous grammar can still fail to be LR(k) for every k.

check.body: Check the converse in $S_1$ with a different grammar from the one in the solution. $S \to aSa \mid bSb \mid a \mid b \mid \epsilon$ is unambiguous, because the outer letters and the parity of the length fix every rule choice. Its language is not deterministic, so no LR(k) parser, and hence no SLR(1) parser, exists for it. Check $S_2$ on small cases: CYK needs 1 split check at $n=2$ and 4 at $n=3$ (two substrings of length 2 with 1 split each, one of length 3 with 2 splits), which matches $(n-1)n(n+1)/6$, a count that stays below $n^3$.

questions.stem: Consider the following context-free grammar where the set of terminals is $\{a,b,c,d,f\}$. $S \to daT \mid Rf$; $T \to aS \mid baT \mid \epsilon$; $R \to caTR \mid \epsilon$. The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table. Which one of the following choices represents the correct combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table ("blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty)?

solutionDiagram.alt: The completed LL(1) table: S to Rf under c and f, T to epsilon under c, f and dollar, with FIRST(Rf) and FOLLOW(T) worked out above it

steps.title: What an LL(1) table cell holds, and the rule that fills it
steps.body: A top-down parser keeps a stack. When a nonterminal $A$ is on top and the next input token is $t$, the table cell $M[A, t]$ names the one rule to expand $A$ with; a blank cell means a syntax error. Three terms fill it. $\mathrm{FIRST}(\alpha)$ is the set of terminals that can start a string derived from $\alpha$. A symbol is nullable if it can derive the empty string $\epsilon$. $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$ is the set of terminals that can come right after $A$ in some derivation from the start symbol, with $\$$ marking the end of input. The rule: put $A \to \alpha$ in $M[A, t]$ for every $t$ in $\mathrm{FIRST}(\alpha)$; and if $\alpha$ is nullable, also for every $t$ in $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$.

steps.title: FIRST of the two S rules
steps.body: $R \to \epsilon$ makes $R$ nullable, and $\mathrm{FIRST}(R) = \{c\}$ since $R \to caTR$ starts with $c$. For the right side $Rf$: start with $\mathrm{FIRST}(R) = \{c\}$; because $R$ can vanish, the next symbol $f$ can come first, so add $f$. The other rule $S \to daT$ starts with $d$.

steps.title: Cells (1) and (2)
steps.body: Cell (1) is $M[S, c]$ and cell (2) is $M[S, f]$. Both $c$ and $f$ are in $\mathrm{FIRST}(Rf)$, so both hold $S \to Rf$. The given $S \to daT$ under $d$ is consistent. Options (B) and (D) (blank at (1)) and option (C) (blank at (2)) are already out.

steps.title: FOLLOW sets for the empty rule
steps.body: $T \to \epsilon$ goes under $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(T)$. $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(R)$: $S \to Rf$ puts $f$ after $R$, and $R \to caTR$ ends in $R$, adding nothing new, so it is $\{f\}$. $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(S)$ and $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(T)$ start from $\$$ (start symbol) and are tied together: $S \to daT$ ends in $T$, so $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(S) \subseteq \mathrm{FOLLOW}(T)$, and $T \to aS$ ends in $S$, so $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(T) \subseteq \mathrm{FOLLOW}(S)$. In $R \to caTR$ the $T$ is followed by $R$, giving $\mathrm{FIRST}(R) = \{c\}$, and since $R$ is nullable also $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(R) = \{f\}$.

steps.title: Cells (3) and (4), and the answer
steps.body: $T \to \epsilon$ goes under $c$, $f$ and $\$$, so cell (3) $= M[T, c]$ holds $T \to \epsilon$, and cell (4) $= M[T, \$]$ holds $T \to \epsilon$ (the table already shows it under $f$). The other $T$ rules start with $a$ and $b$, so no cell has two rules and the grammar is LL(1). The combination is (1) $S \to Rf$, (2) $S \to Rf$, (3) $T \to \epsilon$, (4) $T \to \epsilon$, which is option (A). A script that built the whole table from FIRST and FOLLOW produced exactly these cells.

shortcut.body: Only FIRST is needed. $R$ can vanish, so $\mathrm{FIRST}(Rf)=\{c,f\}$ and $S \to Rf$ belongs in both cell (1) (column $c$) and cell (2) (column $f$). Neither is blank, which leaves only option (A). Check (3) and (4) afterwards if time allows: they hold $T \to \epsilon$ because $c$ and $\$$ are in $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(T)$. Safe because (A) is the only option with both (1) and (2) filled.

traps.text: Treating $R$ as if it always vanishes, so only $f$ can start $Rf$ and cell (1) stays blank. But $R$ can also start with $c$ through $R \to caTR$, so column $c$ gets $S \to Rf$ as well.

Taking $\mathrm{FIRST}(Rf)$ as $\{c\}$ only, which blanks (2) because a nullable $R$ also exposes $f$, and not entering $T \to \epsilon$ under $c$, which blanks (3). An $\epsilon$ rule goes under every symbol of $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(T)$, and $c$ is one of them.

Building the table from FIRST sets alone, so $T \to \epsilon$ never enters under $c$ or $\$$ and (3), (4) stay blank. Entries for $T \to \epsilon$ come from $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(T)=\{\$,c,f\}$. Blank (1) repeats the slip of ignoring $c$ in $\mathrm{FIRST}(Rf)$.

recognize.clues: The question hands over a partly filled parsing table and asks for the missing cells, and the grammar has $\epsilon$ rules ($T \to \epsilon$ and $R \to \epsilon$) whose cells depend on FOLLOW columns, including the end marker.
recognize.contrast: FIRST and FOLLOW questions ask only for the sets. Here the sets are a means: the answer is which rule sits in which cell, and a cell is blank only when neither FIRST nor FOLLOW puts a rule there.

check.body: Trace short sentences and see which rule the parser must pick. The string $f$ comes from $S \to Rf$ with $R$ empty, so with $S$ on top and $f$ next the parser needs that rule. The string $caf$ comes from $S \to Rf \to caTRf$ with $T$ and $R$ empty, so with $S$ on top and $c$ next it needs $S \to Rf$ again, and with $T$ on top and $f$ next it needs $T \to \epsilon$. The string $da$ comes from $S \to daT$ with $T$ empty, so $T$ on top with the end of input next needs $T \to \epsilon$.

questions.stem: Consider the following grammar. $S \to aSB \mid d$; $B \to b$. The number of reduction steps taken by a bottom-up parser while accepting the string $aaadbbb$ is __________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Parse tree of aaadbbb with its seven reductions numbered in parser order, beside the 14-line shift and reduce trace that ends with S on the stack

steps.title: What a bottom-up parser does, and what counts as a reduction
steps.body: A bottom-up parser keeps a stack. Shift moves the next input token onto the stack. Reduce looks at the top of the stack: when the symbols there match the right side of a rule (this piece is called the handle), it replaces them with the rule's left side. The parser accepts when all input is read and the stack holds just the start symbol $S$. Each reduction builds exactly one interior node of the parse tree, and the reductions read backwards form a rightmost derivation. So the number of reductions equals the number of rule applications in the derivation, which equals the number of interior nodes of the parse tree.

steps.title: Shape of the string and the derivation
steps.body: Rule $S \to aSB$ wraps one $a$ on the left and one $B$ on the right of an inner $S$, and $B \to b$ turns each $B$ into a $b$. So the language is $a^n d\, b^n$, and $aaadbbb$ has $n = 3$. Derive it, always rewriting the rightmost nonterminal. Each arrow is one rule application, 7 in all.
steps.tex: S \Rightarrow aSB \Rightarrow aSb \Rightarrow aaSBb \Rightarrow aaSbb \Rightarrow aaaSBbb \Rightarrow aaaSbbb \Rightarrow aaadbbb

steps.title: Run the parser and watch the stack
steps.body: Shift $a$, $a$, $a$, $d$: the stack is $aaad$. Handle $d$: reduce $S \to d$, stack $aaaS$ (reduction 1). Shift $b$: $aaaSb$. Reduce $B \to b$: $aaaSB$ (2). Now the top three symbols $aSB$ match $S \to aSB$: reduce, stack $aaS$ (3). Shift $b$, reduce $B \to b$ (4), reduce $S \to aSB$ (5): stack $aS$. Shift $b$, reduce $B \to b$ (6), reduce $S \to aSB$ (7): stack $S$, input empty, accept. The drawing numbers each node by the reduction that creates it.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Reductions: $S \to d$ once, $B \to b$ three times (one per $b$), $S \to aSB$ three times (one per $a$). Shifts are not counted (there are 7 of them as well, but the question asks only for reductions), and accepting is not a reduction.

shortcut.body: The strings are $a^n d\, b^n$. One reduction per $b$ ($B \to b$), one per $a$ ($S \to aSB$) and one for $d$: $2n+1$ with $n=3$ gives 7. Safe here because the grammar has no $\epsilon$ or unit rules, so every reduction consumes tokens or builds a distinct node.

traps.text: Answering 6: counting only $B \to b$ and $S \to aSB$ and forgetting $S \to d$, which turns the lone $d$ into the innermost $S$.
Answering 14: counting every parser action, shifts included (7 shifts plus 7 reductions). The question asks only for reduction steps.
Answering 3 or 4: counting only the $S \to aSB$ steps, or only the $S$ reductions; the three $B \to b$ steps are reductions too.
Answering 8: adding the final accept action as one more reduction. Accept is not a reduction.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the number of reduction steps a bottom-up parser takes on one given string. No table or lookahead is involved, so only the handles that get reduced matter.
recognize.contrast: A top-down parser expands rules from the start symbol and a bottom-up parser reduces from the tokens, but both use the same rule applications. Shifts are separate moves and must not be added to the count.

check.body: Try smaller strings of the same shape. For $adb$ the parser reduces $d$, then $b$, then $aSB$, which is 3 reductions. For $aadbb$ it is 5. Each added pair of $a$ and $b$ adds exactly two reductions, so the count for the given string follows from the pattern.

questions.stem: Which one of the following kinds of derivation is used by LR parsers?

solutionDiagram.alt: A rightmost derivation of id plus id read downward through five sentential forms, and the same four rules read upward as the reductions of an LR parser

steps.title: Derivations, and the two orders
steps.body: A derivation starts from the start symbol and, one step at a time, replaces a nonterminal by the right side of one of its rules until only tokens remain. In a leftmost derivation the nonterminal replaced at every step is the leftmost one; in a rightmost derivation it is the rightmost one. A parser works backwards or forwards: a top-down parser guesses rules from the start symbol and follows a derivation forwards; a bottom-up parser starts from the tokens and reduces (undoes a rule), so it follows a derivation backwards. The letters in 'LR' say: scan input Left to right, build a Rightmost derivation in reverse.

steps.title: Why the order has to be rightmost
steps.body: The parser reads left to right, and its current sentential form is the stack followed by the unread tokens. A reduction happens at the top of the stack, so everything to the right of the handle is still unread tokens, which are terminals. A rule that was applied last in a derivation, and that has only terminals to its right, is by definition the rightmost nonterminal being rewritten. So the reductions the parser performs, first to last, are the rightmost derivation steps listed last to first.

steps.title: Check on a small case
steps.body: Grammar $E \to E + T \mid T$, $T \to \mathrm{id}$, input $\mathrm{id} + \mathrm{id}$. A script ran an SLR parser and recorded the reductions $T \to \mathrm{id}$, $E \to T$, $T \to \mathrm{id}$, $E \to E + T$. Reversed they are the steps of the rightmost derivation below, and at each step the nonterminal rewritten is the rightmost one.

steps.title: The options
steps.body: Leftmost derivations belong to LL parsers (top-down). 'Rightmost' forwards is the order of a top-down rightmost expansion, which no table-driven parser uses. The match is 'Rightmost in reverse', option (D).

shortcut.body: Read the name: LL(1) is Left-to-right scan with a Leftmost derivation; LR(1) is Left-to-right scan with a Rightmost derivation in reverse. About 10 seconds.

traps.text: Picking leftmost: that is the derivation an LL (top-down) parser follows. LR parsers work bottom-up.
Combining 'bottom-up means reverse' with the left-to-right scan and answering leftmost in reverse. The 'L' in LR names the scan direction, not the derivation; the derivation is rightmost.
Picking rightmost without the reversal: the parser builds the tree from the leaves, so the rule applied last in the derivation is its first reduction.

recognize.clues: The question names LR parsers and asks which derivation they use, with four options pairing leftmost or rightmost with forward or reverse order. It asks what a reduction means, not how any table is built.
recognize.contrast: An LL parser guesses a rule before it has read the tokens that rule covers, so it follows its derivation forwards. An LR parser decides after reading them, so the direction of the derivation it follows flips.

check.body: Test on a grammar with two nonterminals in one line, $S \to AB$, $A \to a$, $B \to b$, and input $ab$. The parser reduces $a$ to $A$, then $b$ to $B$, then $AB$ to $S$. Reversed, that list reads $S \to AB$, $B \to b$, $A \to a$, which rewrites $B$ before $A$, so it is not a leftmost derivation. In the order the parser makes them, the first rule is one for $A$, which cannot start a derivation from $S$.

A derivation is a list of rule applications from the start symbol to the tokens. A leftmost one always rewrites the leftmost nonterminal and a rightmost one always rewrites the rightmost nonterminal.
A bottom-up parser performs reductions, and each reduction undoes one rule application. The steps it performs therefore make up a derivation read in one particular direction.
Take a tiny grammar and a short input, list the reductions in the order the parser makes them, then write the derivation those reductions undo and see which nonterminal each step rewrites.

The rightmost derivation uses the same rules in the opposite order, as in option 1: the rightmost nonterminal $T$ is rewritten before the $E$ on its left. Option 0 is the parser order left unreversed, and option 2 is the leftmost derivation. A script that generated both derivations confirmed the sequences. questions.stem: Consider the grammar given below: $S \to Aa$; $A \to BD$; $B \to b \mid \epsilon$; $D \to d \mid \epsilon$. Let $a$, $b$, $d$, and $\$$ be indexed as in the table. Compute the FOLLOW set of the non-terminal $B$ and write the index values for the symbols in the FOLLOW set in the descending order. (For example, if the FOLLOW set is $\{a, b, d, \$\}$, then the answer should be 3210.) Answer: ________.

steps.title: What FOLLOW means and how it is built
steps.body: $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(X)$ is the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the right of $X$ in some sentential form derived from the start symbol; $\$$ stands for the end of input and belongs to the FOLLOW of the start symbol. A symbol is nullable if it can derive the empty string $\epsilon$. The rule: for every rule $A \to \alpha X \beta$, add $\mathrm{FIRST}(\beta)$ (leaving out $\epsilon$) to $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(X)$; and if $\beta$ is empty or can derive $\epsilon$, also add all of $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$, because whatever follows $A$ then follows $X$ directly.

steps.title: Where B occurs
steps.body: $B$ appears on a right side once, in $A \to BD$, so $\alpha$ is empty and $\beta = D$. $\mathrm{FIRST}(D) = \{d\}$, so $d \in \mathrm{FOLLOW}(B)$. $D \to \epsilon$ makes $D$ nullable, so $B$ can sit right at the end of what $A$ produces, and $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$ is also added.

steps.title: FOLLOW of A
steps.body: $A$ appears once, in $S \to Aa$, followed by the terminal $a$. So $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A) = \{a\}$.

steps.title: Combine and encode
steps.body: $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(B) = \{d\} \cup \{a\} = \{a, d\}$. The symbol $b$ is not there (nothing puts $b$ after $B$) and $\$$ is not there ($\$$ follows only the start symbol $S$, which never appears on a right side). Indices: $a$ is 3 and $d$ is 1. In descending order the answer is 31.

shortcut.body: Find where $B$ stands: only in $A \to BD$. What can come next is $d$ (from $D$), or, if $D$ vanishes, whatever follows $A$, which is $a$. Two symbols, indices 3 and 1: 31. Unsafe if $D$ were not nullable: then $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$ would not be added.

traps.text: Answering 1: taking $\mathrm{FIRST}(D)=\{d\}$ and forgetting that $D$ can vanish, so $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)=\{a\}$ must be added.
Answering 321 or 21: putting $b$ into the set, by confusing $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(B)$ with $\mathrm{FIRST}(B)$.

Answering 310: adding $\$$ because $B$ sits inside a derivation from $S$. $\$$ is in $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(S)$ only, and it reaches $B$ only through a chain of nullable tails; here $S \to Aa$ ends in the terminal $a$, which blocks it.
Answering 3: missing the $d$ coming from $\mathrm{FIRST}(D)$.

recognize.clues: The question asks for a FOLLOW set by name. The grammar has $\epsilon$ rules for $B$ and $D$, so a nullable symbol stands after $B$ and the FOLLOW set of the left side must be pulled in.
recognize.contrast: FIRST asks what a string can start with. FOLLOW looks at the neighbours on the right of a symbol, so the rules of $B$ itself ($b$ or $\epsilon$) do not enter its FOLLOW set.

check.body: List the strings the grammar derives: $a$, $ba$, $da$ and $bda$. Wherever $B$ produced $b$, the next symbol is $d$ or $a$. Wherever $B$ produced nothing, the symbol standing in its place is also $d$ or $a$. The symbol $b$ never stands right after $B$, and the end of input never does either.
