questions.stem: Consider the augmented grammar given below: $S' \to S$; $S \to \langle L \rangle \mid \mathrm{id}$; $L \to L, S \mid S$. Let $I_0 = \mathrm{CLOSURE}(\{[S' \to \bullet S]\})$. The number of items in the set $\mathrm{GOTO}(I_0, \langle)$ is: ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: State I0 with three items, and GOTO(I0, less-than) with five items: the kernel S to less-than dot L greater-than plus two L items and two S items from closure

steps.title: Items, closure and GOTO
steps.body: An item is a rule with a dot marking how much of the right side the parser has already seen, such as $S \to \langle \bullet L \rangle$. The grammar is augmented with $S' \to S$ so there is one start item. $\mathrm{CLOSURE}(I)$ adds, for every item with the dot directly before a nonterminal $B$, all rules of $B$ with the dot at the start, and repeats until nothing new appears. $\mathrm{GOTO}(I, X)$ takes every item of $I$ that has $X$ right after the dot, moves the dot over $X$, and closes the result. The symbols $\langle$, $\rangle$ and the comma are terminals here.

steps.title: Build I0
steps.body: Start with $S' \to \bullet S$. The dot is before $S$, so add $S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle$ and $S \to \bullet \mathrm{id}$. No dot is before $L$, so $I_0$ has 3 items.

steps.title: Move the dot over the opening bracket
steps.body: Among the items of $I_0$ only $S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle$ has $\langle$ after the dot. Moving the dot gives the single kernel item $S \to \langle \bullet L \rangle$.

steps.title: Close it
steps.body: The dot is before $L$: add both $L$ rules, $L \to \bullet L, S$ and $L \to \bullet S$. The item $L \to \bullet S$ has the dot before $S$: add both $S$ rules, $S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle$ and $S \to \bullet \mathrm{id}$. $L \to \bullet L, S$ puts the dot before $L$ again, which adds nothing new. The set is $\{S \to \langle \bullet L \rangle,\ L \to \bullet L, S,\ L \to \bullet S,\ S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle,\ S \to \bullet \mathrm{id}\}$: 5 items. A script that built the automaton gave the same set.

shortcut.body: After the dot passes $\langle$ it sits before $L$, and $L \to \bullet S$ then exposes $S$: so the state is the 1 kernel item plus all $L$ rules (2) plus all $S$ rules (2) = 5. The $S'$ item never comes back. Safe because both nonterminals are added in full.

traps.text: Answering 1: moving the dot and stopping, without taking the closure.
Answering 3: closing over $L$ only. $L \to \bullet S$ exposes $S$, so the two $S$ rules must be added as well.
Answering 6: including $S' \to \bullet S$ from $I_0$. Only the items that had $\langle$ after the dot move, and $S' \to \bullet S$ did not.
Answering 4: leaving out $S \to \bullet \langle L \rangle$ in the closure, forgetting that brackets can nest.

recognize.clues: The grammar is augmented with $S'$, the set $I_0$ is named through CLOSURE, and the question asks for the size of a GOTO state. That is automaton construction, not a parsing decision.
recognize.contrast: SLR(1) uses the same automaton, and LR(1) items would add a lookahead so the same rule could be counted once per lookahead. Here the items are plain LR(0) items with no lookahead.

check.body: Test that the set you found is closed. Take each item with the dot before a nonterminal and confirm that every rule of that nonterminal is present with the dot at the start. Then confirm that no item has the dot before the closing bracket or the comma, since those add nothing. If every test passes the set is closed, and dropping any item breaks one of the tests.

steps.title: Precedence and associativity, read from a tree
steps.body: In a parse tree for an expression every interior node is an operator applied to its two children, and the tree is evaluated from the bottom up: the deeper the node, the earlier it runs. Precedence decides which of two different operators groups first, so the operator that sits lower in the tree has the higher precedence. Associativity decides which of two equal operators in a row groups first. If the chain leans left, so that $x \mathbin{op} y \mathbin{op} z$ is $(x \mathbin{op} y) \mathbin{op} z$, the operator is left associative; if it leans right, giving $x \mathbin{op} (y \mathbin{op} z)$, it is right associative. Rule: look at where each operator's own nodes sit, then at which side the chain leans.

steps.title: Precedence of dollar versus hash
steps.body: The \$ nodes form a subtree that hangs below a # node (the left child of the middle #), and no # node is ever inside a \$ subtree. The \$ subtree is the operand of #, so it runs first: \$ has higher precedence than #.

steps.title: Associativity of dollar
steps.body: The \$ subtree is $\$(\$(b, c), d)$: the inner \$ is the left child of the outer one. The two \$ operators group as $(b \mathbin{\$} c) \mathbin{\$} d$, so \$ is left associative.

steps.title: Associativity of #
steps.body: The # operators are the root, the second # and the third #. The root has # as its right child, and the second # has # as its right child: the chain leans right and groups as $a \mathbin{\#} (X \mathbin{\#} (e \mathbin{\#} f))$ with $X = (b \mathbin{\$} c) \mathbin{\$} d$. So # is right associative.

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body: The facts are: \$ higher precedence, \$ left associative, # right associative. That is option (A). A script that parsed a#b\$c\$d#e#f by precedence climbing under each option's rules rebuilt exactly this tree for (A) and a different tree for (B), (C) and (D).

shortcut.body: Read the tree twice. Chains: the \$ chain leans left, the # chain leans right, which already matches (A) and (D). Precedence: the \$ subtree is below #, so \$ binds tighter, which picks (A) and rejects (D). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Reading the root operator # as the one that binds tightest because it is at the top of the picture. The root runs last, so # has the lower precedence.
Calling # left associative. The # chain a, X, (e#f) leans right: each # has the next # as its right child, so # is right associative.
Getting both associativities right but reversing precedence, by the same 'top of the tree binds tightest' error as in (B). The \$ subtree is deeper, so it binds tighter.

recognize.clues: A parse tree is given for an expression with two binary operators, and the options pair a precedence order with an associativity for each operator. Both facts must be read off the shape of the tree.
recognize.contrast: A grammar with no precedence rules is ambiguous and has many trees. Here the tree is already fixed, so the job is to read the rules off it, not to choose among trees.

check.body: Flip one rule at a time and see whether the tree could still be drawn. If the \$ chain leaned the other way, $b \mathbin{\$} c \mathbin{\$} d$ would group as $b \mathbin{\$} (c \mathbin{\$} d)$, which needs $c$ and $d$ under one \$ node. The tree does not show that, so the first claim about \$ cannot be reversed. Do the same flip for the # chain and for the precedence.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about parser is/are CORRECT? I. Canonical LR is more powerful than SLR. II. SLR is more powerful than LALR. III. SLR is more powerful than Canonical LR.

solutionDiagram.alt: Canonical LR(1) contains LALR(1) which contains SLR(1), with the L = R grammar inside LALR but outside SLR, and a second grammar inside canonical LR but outside LALR

steps.title: What 'more powerful' means, and what separates the three parsers
steps.body: A parser is more powerful when the set of grammars it can handle without table conflicts is larger. SLR(1), LALR(1) and canonical LR(1) all build the same kind of shift-reduce table from LR items. They differ in the lookahead that allows a reduce. SLR uses $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$, which ignores the state. LALR uses the exact lookaheads of canonical LR but merges states with the same core, pooling their lookaheads. Canonical LR keeps one state per item-and-lookahead context and uses the exact lookahead. Exact lookaheads are always a subset of the pooled ones, which are a subset of FOLLOW; fewer reduce entries means fewer conflicts. So SLR(1) grammars $\subset$ LALR(1) grammars $\subset$ LR(1) grammars.

steps.title: Statement I
steps.body: The grammar $S \to L = R \mid R$, $L \to {*}R \mid \mathrm{id}$, $R \to L$ has an SLR conflict (on $=$, since $=\ \in \mathrm{FOLLOW}(R)$), but canonical LR(1) reduces $R \to L$ only on $\$$ there and has none. A script confirmed 1 conflicting cell for SLR and 0 for canonical LR. Every SLR(1) grammar is also canonical LR(1). So canonical LR is strictly more powerful: I is true.

steps.title: Statements II and III
steps.body: The same grammar is LALR(1) (0 conflicts) but not SLR(1), so LALR handles a grammar SLR cannot: II is false. It is also canonical LR(1) but not SLR(1), so III is false. A script over 6000 random grammars found none that was SLR-clean but LALR-conflicting, and none that was SLR-clean but LR(1)-conflicting. Only I is true: option (A).

shortcut.body: Memorise the order SLR $<$ LALR $<$ canonical LR in power. A statement that puts a weaker parser above a stronger one is false, so II and III fall and only I remains. Safe: the nesting is strict and holds for every grammar.

traps.text: Thinking SLR beats LALR because SLR is 'simpler' or has a smaller table. Smaller does not mean stronger: LALR keeps better lookaheads, so it accepts every grammar SLR accepts and more.
Putting SLR above canonical LR. Canonical LR has the largest class, at the cost of the most states.
Reversing the whole hierarchy, which makes both II and III look true. Both reverse the correct order.

recognize.clues: Three statements compare SLR, LALR and canonical LR by power, so the question is about how the three grammar classes nest, not about building any one table.
recognize.contrast: Do not swap the two kinds of lost precision. LALR loses some by merging states with equal cores, while SLR loses more by ignoring the state and using FOLLOW.

check.body: Run the three constructions on two grammars. For $S \to L = R \mid R$, $L \to {*}R \mid \mathrm{id}$, $R \to L$ a script found 1 SLR conflict and none for LALR or canonical LR. For $S \to aAd \mid bBd \mid aBe \mid bAe$, $A \to c$, $B \to c$ it found none for canonical LR but 2 for LALR, because merging the two states that contain the rules for $c$ pools their lookaheads. Together the two grammars separate the three classes.

questions.stem: Consider the following expression grammar $G$: $E \to E - T \mid T$; $T \to T + F \mid F$; $F \to (E) \mid \mathrm{id}$. Which of the following grammars is not left recursive, but is equivalent to $G$?
options: $E \to E - T \mid T$; $T \to T + F \mid F$; $F \to (E) \mid \mathrm{id}$

steps.title: Left recursion, why it matters, and the standard repair
steps.body: A nonterminal $A$ is left recursive if $A \Rightarrow^+ A\alpha$ for some $\alpha$: in the simplest case a rule $A \to A\alpha$ whose right side starts with $A$ itself. A top-down (recursive-descent or LL) parser expanding $A$ would call itself on $A$ without consuming a token and never stop. Two grammars are equivalent when they generate exactly the same set of strings. The repair: replace $A \to A\alpha \mid \beta$ by $A \to \beta A'$ and $A' \to \alpha A' \mid \epsilon$. Both versions generate $\beta$ followed by zero or more $\alpha$, so the language is unchanged. The question therefore has two checks per option: no nonterminal is left recursive, and the language is that of $G$.

steps.title: Repair G by hand
steps.body: $E \to E - T \mid T$ has $\alpha = {-}T$ and $\beta = T$: it becomes $E \to TX$, $X \to -TX \mid \epsilon$. $T \to T + F \mid F$ has $\alpha = {+}F$ and $\beta = F$: it becomes $T \to FY$, $Y \to +FY \mid \epsilon$. $F$ is not left recursive and stays. This is exactly option (C).

steps.title: Reject the others
steps.body: Option (A) is $G$ itself, which is left recursive in both $E$ and $T$. Option (B) repairs $E$ but keeps $T \to T + F$, so $T$ is still left recursive. Option (D) has no left recursion, but it generates a smaller language: its only operand is $\mathrm{id}$ (the $F \to (E)$ rule is gone), parentheses can appear only once around the whole expression, and it cannot derive $((\mathrm{id}))$ or $(\mathrm{id}) - \mathrm{id}$. A script enumerated every string of at most 9 tokens: $G$ has 257, option (C) has the same 257, and (D) misses 211 of them. A left-recursion check flagged $E$, $T$ in (A), $T$ in (B), and nothing in (C) or (D).

shortcut.body: Scan each option for a rule whose right side begins with the left side's own name: $E \to E\ldots$ or $T \to T\ldots$. (A) has both, (B) still has $T \to T + F$. That leaves (C) and (D); (D) has dropped $F \to (E)$ entirely, so it cannot nest parentheses, which $G$ can. (C) remains. Safe because the check is purely syntactic.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because it is trivially equivalent to $G$. It is the same grammar, and it is left recursive, so it fails the other half of the question.
Stopping after removing the left recursion of $E$ and forgetting that $T \to T + F$ has the same fault. Every nonterminal must be checked.
Choosing (D) because it is short and clearly not left recursive. It changes the language (no nested parentheses, only $\mathrm{id}$ operands), so it is not equivalent to $G$.

recognize.clues: The grammar has rules such as $E \to E - T$ and the question asks for an equivalent grammar with no left recursion. The options differ in which nonterminals were repaired and in what else was changed.
recognize.contrast: Left factoring removes a shared prefix so a parser need not backtrack, which is a different repair. The defect here is a rule that begins with its own left side, not a shared prefix.

check.body: Derive the string $\mathrm{id} + \mathrm{id} - \mathrm{id}$ in $G$ and then in the grammar you chose. In $G$ it takes $E \to E - T$ and $T \to T + F$. In a correct repair the same string comes from $E \to TX$, a $Y$ chain for the plus, and an $X$ chain for the minus, with both chains ending in $\epsilon$. Also derive $(\mathrm{id})$: a grammar that cannot do it has lost the bracket rule.

questions.stem: Consider the following grammar: $P \to xQRS$; $Q \to yz \mid z$; $R \to w \mid \epsilon$; $S \to y$. What is $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(Q)$?

steps.title: What FOLLOW means and how it is built
steps.body: $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(X)$ is the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the right of $X$ in some sentential form derived from the start symbol; $\$$ marks the end of input and goes in the FOLLOW of the start symbol only. A symbol is nullable if it can derive the empty string $\epsilon$. The rule: for every rule $A \to \alpha X \beta$, add $\mathrm{FIRST}(\beta)$ (without $\epsilon$) to $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(X)$; if everything in $\beta$ is nullable (or $\beta$ is empty), also add $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(A)$.

steps.title: Find where Q appears
steps.body: $Q$ is on a right side once, in $P \to xQRS$. What follows $Q$ is $\beta = RS$.

steps.title: Compute FIRST(RS)
steps.body: $\mathrm{FIRST}(R) = \{w\}$ and $R$ is nullable (it can derive $\epsilon$), so the next symbol $S$ can come right after $Q$ and its first terminal counts too: $\mathrm{FIRST}(S) = \{y\}$. $S$ is not nullable, so the walk stops there and $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(P)$, which holds $\$$, is not added.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: $\{w, y\}$ is option (C). A script computing the FOLLOW sets of all four nonterminals gave $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(Q)=\{w,y\}$.

shortcut.body: Look at the one rule where $Q$ appears: $xQRS$. After $Q$ comes $R$, which is $w$ or nothing; if nothing, $S$ starts with $y$. So $\{w, y\}$. Unsafe when $S$ could also vanish, because then $\mathrm{FOLLOW}(P)$ would join in; here $S \to y$ cannot.

traps.text: Writing the nonterminal $R$. FOLLOW sets contain terminals (and $\$$), never nonterminals.
Answering $\{w\}$: using $\mathrm{FIRST}(R)$ and forgetting that $R \to \epsilon$ lets $S$ (and so $y$) come directly after $Q$.
Adding $\$$ because $Q$ is near the end of the rule. $\$$ would join only if both $R$ and $S$ were nullable and $\$ \in \mathrm{FOLLOW}(P)$; $S \to y$ is not nullable, so $\$$ stays out.

recognize.clues: The stem asks for FOLLOW of one nonterminal that occurs once, followed by a nullable symbol ($R \to w \mid \epsilon$) and then a non-nullable one ($S \to y$). The nullable symbol in the middle is the cue to keep reading.
recognize.contrast: FIRST of the string after $Q$ is not the same as FIRST of $R$ alone: FIRST needs the nullable check, and \$ enters FOLLOW only when the whole tail is nullable, which a terminal-only $S$ prevents.

check.body: Test by deriving sentential forms from $P$. Choosing $R \to w$ gives $x\,Q\,w\,y$ with $w$ next to $Q$, and choosing $R \to \epsilon$ gives $x\,Q\,y$ with $y$ next to $Q$. No derivation ends right after $Q$, because $S \to y$ always follows, so \$ never touches $Q$.

questions.stem: Consider the following grammar (shown below), where relop is a relational operator (e.g., $<$, $>$, ...), $\grave{o}$ refers to the empty statement, and if, then, else are terminals. Consider a program $P$ following the above grammar containing ten if terminals. The number of control flow paths in $P$ is __________. For example, the program if $e_1$ then $e_2$ else $e_3$ has 2 control flow paths, $e_1 \to e_2$ and $e_1 \to e_3$.

code.text:
stmt   -> if expr then expr else expr; stmt | ò
expr   -> term relop term | term
term   -> id | number
id     -> a | b | c
number -> [0-9]

solutionDiagram.alt: Control flow of consecutive ifs: each cond splits into then and else, both rejoin at the next cond, so the number of paths goes 1, 2, 4 and reaches 2 to the power 10 at the exit

steps.title: What a program from the grammar looks like, and what a path is
steps.body: A grammar generates programs: start from $\mathrm{stmt}$ and keep replacing nonterminals with a rule's right side until only terminals remain. A control flow path is one route a run can take through the program from its start to its end, written as the sequence of expressions evaluated; the example shows an if with 2 paths because the run takes either the then-branch or the else-branch. Rule for counting: paths multiply across statements that run one after another, and add across alternatives at the same point.

steps.title: Where the ifs can sit
steps.body: The word $\mathrm{if}$ occurs in exactly one rule, $\mathrm{stmt} \to \mathrm{if}\ \mathrm{expr}\ \mathrm{then}\ \mathrm{expr}\ \mathrm{else}\ \mathrm{expr};\ \mathrm{stmt}$. The three $\mathrm{expr}$ parts derive only $\mathrm{term}$, $\mathrm{relop}$ and $\mathrm{id}$ or $\mathrm{number}$, never a $\mathrm{stmt}$. The only $\mathrm{stmt}$ on the right side is the trailing one. So an if can never sit inside another if: a program with ten ifs applies the first rule ten times and then $\mathrm{stmt} \to \grave{o}$, giving ten ifs one after another.

steps.title: Count the paths
steps.body: Each if lets the run go through the then-part or the else-part, and both continue to the next statement. The expressions use $\mathrm{relop}$ without any short-circuit, so each expression is one step on a path. Every if therefore doubles the number of paths. A script built the control flow graph for $k$ ifs in a row and counted routes: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 for $k = 1, \dots, 10$.

shortcut.body: Ifs in sequence double the path count each time, so $n$ ifs give $2^n$ paths and ten give $2^{10}=1024$. This is safe only because the grammar forbids nesting; with nested ifs the counts would add instead of multiply.

traps.text: Answering 20: adding 2 per if, as if each if were an alternative of the whole program. Statements in sequence multiply their choices.
Answering 512 or 2048: an off-by-one in the exponent, using $2^9$ (counting only the ifs after the first) or $2^{11}$ (counting the empty statement as one more split).
Answering 100 or 10: treating the ten ifs as ten independent places each with 10 options, or counting only the ifs themselves.
Answering 1023: subtracting one path as the 'all else' or 'all then' case. Both are real paths, so every combination of the ten choices counts.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a grammar and asks about programs it generates, so the work is reading which derivations are possible. The tell is that $\mathrm{stmt}$ appears on a right side only as the trailing item, so ifs chain and never nest.
recognize.contrast: This is about what the grammar generates, not about parsing it or its ambiguity. A grammar that allowed $\mathrm{stmt}$ inside the branches would nest ifs, and path counts would then add inside a branch instead of multiplying.

check.body: Use the recurrence $p(k)=2\,p(k-1)$ with $p(0)=1$ for the empty program. Second route: a path is fixed by writing then or else for each of the ten ifs in order, and all such choice strings are distinct paths, which is the number of binary strings of length 10.
